questions.q: Zoya strikes a tuning fork gently on a rubber pad. She cannot see the prongs move, so her friend says they are not vibrating. Zoya touches one prong to the surface of water in a tray and ripples spread out from the point of contact. What do the ripples tell Zoya?
questions.a: The prong is vibrating, even though the movement is too quick to see directly
o: The prong is vibrating, even though the movement is too quick to see directly
The water in the tray is itself the source of the sound that she hears from the fork
The prong has stopped vibrating the moment that it touched the surface of the water
The sound of the fork can be heard only after the prong has touched the water

questions.q: A grasshopper is held in a glass jar. A student pins its wings and legs so that neither can rub against anything, and the insect, which was chirping loudly, goes quiet. Which reading of this observation fits the chapter?
questions.a: Its chirp comes from body parts rubbing, so stopping the rubbing removes the sound
o: Its chirp comes from body parts rubbing, so stopping the rubbing removes the sound
Grasshoppers produce their sound with vocal cords, which the pins must have damaged
Sound is produced by an animal only when it is frightened by being held in a jar
A grasshopper can make its sound only while it is moving through the open air

questions.q: Which of these set-ups will NOT give any sound, according to the chapter's account of how sound is produced?
questions.a: A rubber band stretched over an open box and left untouched
o: A rubber band stretched over an open box and left untouched
A stretched string that is pulled and then released by a finger
A metal object that is struck hard with a wooden stick
A bansuri with air blown through its hollow pipe

questions.q: Pooja blows steadily across the mouth of a bamboo bansuri and a clear note is heard. According to the chapter, what is vibrating to produce this note?
questions.a: The air inside the hollow pipe
o: The air inside the hollow pipe
The tip of the pipe where her lips touch it
The fingers placed over the holes
The wall of the bamboo pipe, which moves like a string

questions.q: Which of the following motions is a vibration of the kind that produces sound?
questions.a: A plucked stretched string moving to and fro on both sides of its rest position
o: A plucked stretched string moving to and fro on both sides of its rest position
A ball rolling steadily down a slope and coming to rest at the bottom of it
A door pushed once and then left open for the rest of the day
A cycle moving along a straight road at a constant speed for an hour

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A sound produced by a vibrating object stops when the vibration stops.
Statement 2: Vocal cords are tightly stretched muscular flaps located inside the larynx.
Statement 3: In most musical instruments exactly one vibrating part is involved in producing the sound.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: in most musical instruments more than one vibrating part is involved.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
All three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Touching a vibrating prong of a tuning fork to a water surface forms ripples on the water.
Reason (R): Water is the source of the sound that a tuning fork produces.
questions.a: A is true: the ripples show the prong is vibrating. R is false: the source of the sound is the vibrating prong, not the water.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q: After a tuning fork is struck, a student presses a palm firmly on both its prongs and the hum ends at once. The sound stopped because the ___ of the prongs was stopped.
questions.a: vibration

questions.q:
Rohan stretches a rubber band across an open cardboard box and plucks it.
(a) Name the source of the sound he hears.
(b) He now presses a finger firmly on the band right after plucking. What happens to the sound, and why?
questions.a: (a) The vibrating rubber band is the source. (b) The sound stops, because pressing the band stops its vibration and sound lasts only while the vibration continues.
s: (a) Names the vibrating rubber band as the source
(b) Sound stops because the vibration is stopped

questions.q:
(a) Name the part that vibrates when a bansuri is blown.
(b) A string instrument and a drum also make sound. Name the kind of vibrating part in each, using the chapter's list of vibrating things.
questions.a: (a) The air inside the hollow pipe (the air column). (b) A string instrument has vibrating strings; a drum has a vibrating membrane (the drum head).
s: (a) Air inside the pipe vibrates
(b) Strings for the string instrument and membrane for the drum

questions.q: A human speaker and a cricket both produce sound. Differentiate how the sound is produced in each, and state what is common in the two cases.
questions.a: In a human, the vocal cords in the larynx vibrate and the tongue, lips, mouth and nasal cavity help turn the sound into speech or music; a cricket rubs its wings or legs against each other. In both, sound comes from a vibrating source.
s: Human: vibrating vocal cords, helped by tongue, lips, mouth and nasal cavity
Cricket: rubbing wings or legs, and both have a vibrating source

questions.q: Meena says: 'The ripples on the water are the sound of the tuning fork.' (a) Is she right? (b) What is the role of the ripples in Activity 10.2?
questions.a: (a) No, the ripples are not sound; they are waves on the water surface. (b) They show that the prong touching the water is vibrating, which supports the idea that sound is produced by vibrating objects.
s: (a) Says ripples are waves on water, not the sound
(b) Ripples show the prong vibrates

questions.q:
A vibrating object that cannot be seen moving is not a source of sound.
State True or False and give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: False. A tuning fork's prongs vibrate too fast to see directly, yet the ripples they raise on water show that they are vibrating and producing sound.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: vibration can be too quick to see, and ripples reveal it

questions.q: Describe how you would use a tuning fork and a tray of water to show that sound is produced by vibration. Give the way to start the vibration, what you do next and what you observe.
questions.a: Hold the fork by its stem and strike a prong gently on a soft rubber pad (not a hard surface). Bring it to the ear to hear the sound, then touch a vibrating prong gently to the water surface. Ripples form on the water, showing the prong vibrates while the sound is produced.
s: Strikes a prong gently on a rubber pad to start vibration
Hears sound near the ear, then touches the prong to the water
Observes ripples and concludes the prong vibrates as sound is produced

questions.q: Ishaan says: 'A bansuri cannot be a source of sound, because I see no part of it moving.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Claim: No, it is wrong. When a bansuri is blown, the air inside its hollow pipe vibrates and produces the sound. The vibrating part (air) is not visible, so the absence of visible motion does not mean there is no vibration.
s: Verdict: No, the claim is wrong
Names the air inside the pipe as the vibrating source
Explains that not seeing movement does not mean no vibration

questions.q: Priya says: 'Speech is made by the vocal cords alone; the tongue, lips, mouth and nasal cavity do nothing.' Decide whether this is right, wrong or partly right.
questions.a: Partly right. The sound is produced by the vibration of the vocal cords in the larynx, which she has right. But the tongue, lips, mouth and nasal cavity help in converting that sound into speech or music, so they do play a part.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: vocal cords vibrate to produce the sound
Wrong part: the other organs help turn the sound into speech or music

questions.q: A student writes in her notebook: 'I plucked a stretched rubber band and then held it perfectly still, yet its sound continued for a long time.' Show that this record cannot be correct.
questions.a: Sound is produced only while the object vibrates, and it stops once the vibration stops. A rubber band held perfectly still is not vibrating, so it cannot go on producing sound; the record must be wrong.
s: States that sound lasts only as long as the vibration
Notes that a band held still is not vibrating
Concludes the sound cannot continue, so the record is wrong

questions.q: Design three short demonstrations for a Class 6 class, one using a rubber band and a cardboard box, one using a tuning fork and a water tray and one using the throat while singing. For each, say what the class does, what it observes and what the demonstration shows about sound.
questions.a: Rubber band: stretch it across the open box and pluck; sound is heard while it is seen vibrating and stops when the vibration stops, so sound comes from vibration. Tuning fork: strike on a rubber pad and touch a prong to water; ripples form, so the prong is vibrating as it sounds. Throat: touch the throat while singing; vibrations are felt, as the vocal cords in the larynx vibrate.
s: Rubber band: pluck, observe sound only during vibration
Rubber band: concludes sound is produced by vibration
Tuning fork: strike, touch water, ripples seen
Tuning fork: concludes the prong vibrates while sounding
Throat: vibration felt, due to vocal cords in the larynx

questions.q: A teacher says: 'Whether it is a cricket, a person or a flute, every sound has one thing in common at its source.' Justify this statement using the three examples, then give one way in which the three sources differ.
questions.a: In each case something vibrates: the cricket's wings or legs rubbing against each other, the person's vocal cords in the larynx, and the air column inside the flute's hollow pipe. The common thing is therefore a vibrating source. They differ in what vibrates: body parts rubbing, stretched muscular flaps or a column of air.
s: Cricket: rubbing wings or legs vibrate
Person: vocal cords vibrate (larynx)
Flute: air inside hollow pipe vibrates
Common idea: a vibrating source
One correct difference in what vibrates

questions.q:
At a science fair in a Shillong school, three exhibits stand side by side. Exhibit A: a rubber band stretched across an open box which visitors pluck. Exhibit B: a bansuri that a student blows. Exhibit C: a volunteer who hums a note with her fingers resting lightly on her throat. A visitor says he can see nothing moving at B, and so concludes there is no vibration there. Stall rules: only two exhibits may run at the same time because the room is small.
(a) Name what vibrates, and so is the source, at each of the three exhibits.
(b) How would you answer the visitor about B?
(c) What will visitors notice at A when the band stops moving, and what does this show?
(d) Choose which two exhibits should run for a group of young children and say what the group will miss from the exhibit you leave out.
questions.a: (a) A: the rubber band; B: the air inside the pipe; C: the vocal cords in the larynx. (b) The air column inside the hollow pipe vibrates and produces the sound even though it cannot be seen. (c) The sound stops once the band stops vibrating, so sound lasts only while vibration lasts. (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. A and C because the vibration can be seen or felt, missing B where vibration is invisible; or B and C missing the visible band.
s: (a) Band, air in pipe, vocal cords
(b) Air column vibrates though unseen
(c) Sound stops when vibration stops
(d) A reasoned choice naming what the left-out exhibit would have shown

questions.q:
A teacher in a school in Hyderabad has to show 40 Class 9 students that sound is produced by vibration. She has two methods. Method 1: students touch their throat while humming. This needs no equipment. Method 2: she strikes a tuning fork on a rubber pad and touches a prong to a tray of water. The class has only two tuning forks and one tray, so only a few students can see it up close.
(a) What do the students feel in Method 1, and which organ is responsible?
(b) What will the class see in Method 2, and what does it show about the prong?
(c) What happens to the ripples and the sound when the prong stops vibrating?
(d) Choose one method for the whole class and give one advantage and one limit of your choice.
questions.a: (a) They feel a buzzing, caused by the vibrating vocal cords in the larynx. (b) Ripples on the water surface, showing the prong is vibrating. (c) Both stop, because sound and ripples need the vibration to continue. (d) A reasoned choice: Method 1 reaches all 40 students but the vibration is felt not seen; Method 2 shows vibration visibly but only a few can see it up close.
s: (a) Buzzing felt, vocal cords in the larynx
(b) Ripples show the prong vibrating
(c) Sound and ripples stop when vibration stops
(d) Reasoned choice with one advantage and one limit

questions.q: During the vacuum bell jar experiment, Aman's friend watches the electric bell while the pump removes air. The sound fades and she says the bell has stopped working. What should Aman point out?
questions.a: The bell can still be seen ringing, so the sound fades because less and less medium is left to carry it
o: The bell can still be seen ringing, so the sound fades because less and less medium is left to carry it
The bell has stopped ringing, because removing air from the jar cuts off its electric supply
The sound fades because sound travels much faster once the air is removed from the jar
The sound is produced only when air presses against the surface of the ringing bell

questions.q: Two astronauts repairing the arm of a space station stand a metre apart on a spacewalk. One strikes a spanner against the metal arm. Why can the other astronaut not hear the clank directly?
questions.a: Outer space is a near vacuum, so there is no medium for the sound to propagate through
o: Outer space is a near vacuum, so there is no medium for the sound to propagate through
Sound produced by metal objects can travel only inside a closed spacesuit and not outside
Space is too far from the Earth for any vibration of a metal object to occur there
Sound waves do reach the ear from space but only after a very long delay in time

questions.q: Nikhil taps two metal spoons against each other while they are fully submerged in a bucket of water, and hears the tap while standing beside the bucket. Along which path did the sound reach his ear?
questions.a: From the spoons through the water and then through the air to his ear
o: From the spoons through the water and then through the air to his ear
Only through the water, since the spoons are not in contact with the air
Only through the metal of the spoons, since solids carry sound best
Directly through the air, as water does not let sound travel

questions.q: Which of the following cannot act as a medium for sound, according to the chapter?
questions.a: A region of space that contains no matter at all
o: A region of space that contains no matter at all
The steel rail of a long railway track
The water that fills a large swimming pool
The air that fills a closed classroom

questions.q:
Match each situation (column I) with what it shows (column II).
Column I: 1. Meera presses one ear to a desk, closes her other ear, and hears her friend scratch the far edge.  2. Two spoons are tapped together under water in a full bucket and the tap is heard by someone standing outside.  3. A bell's sound fades to almost nothing as a pump removes air from a sealed jar, yet the bell can be seen ringing.  4. Two astronauts on a spacewalk have to use devices fitted in their suits to speak to each other.
Column II: a. Sound needs a medium and fades as the medium is removed  b. Sound can travel through a solid  c. Outer space lacks a medium, so sound cannot propagate there directly  d. Sound can travel through a liquid
questions.a: The desk scratch shows a solid, the submerged spoons show a liquid, the fading bell shows sound needs a medium, and the spacewalk shows that space has no medium.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: In the bell jar experiment, once a near vacuum is reached, the bell can no longer be seen ringing.
Statement 2: When air is let back into the jar, the sound returns and gradually becomes as loud as before.
Statement 3: Astronauts on a spacewalk use special devices fitted into their spacesuits to communicate.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false: even at near vacuum the bell can still be seen ringing, but almost no sound is heard.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
All three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In a bell jar from which most air has been pumped out, a ringing bell can be seen but hardly heard.
Reason (R): Sound needs a material medium to propagate.
questions.a: A is true: the bell can be seen ringing but almost no sound reaches the listener. R is true and explains A, because with little air left there is hardly any medium to carry the sound.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: A sealed jar holds a ringing bell, and almost all the air is then pumped out. The bell is still visible but almost silent because the jar no longer has a ___ to carry the sound.
questions.a: medium

questions.q:
An astronaut on a spacewalk who shouts very loudly will be heard directly by a colleague one metre away.
State True or False and give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: False. Outer space is a near vacuum, so there is no medium for the shout to propagate through, no matter how loud; the astronauts must use special devices fitted in their suits.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: no medium in near vacuum, and loudness cannot replace it

questions.q:
In Activity 10.3, Meera places her ear on a desk and closes her other ear while her friend scratches the desk.
(a) What does she conclude if she hears the scratch?
(b) Why is her other ear closed?
questions.a: (a) Sound can travel through solids, here the wooden desk. (b) Closing the other ear stops her from hearing the sound that comes through the air, so what she hears has travelled through the desk.
s: (a) Sound travels through solids
(b) Closing the other ear removes the sound heard through air

questions.q: In the bell jar experiment, (a) what does the listener notice as air is pumped out, and (b) what is noticed when air is let back in?
questions.a: (a) The sound becomes fainter and fainter, until almost none is heard at near vacuum, although the bell is seen ringing. (b) The sound is heard again and gradually becomes as loud as before.
s: (a) Sound fades to almost nothing while the bell is still seen ringing
(b) Sound returns gradually to its earlier loudness

questions.q: Differentiate between a medium and a vacuum with respect to sound, giving one example of a medium from the chapter's activities.
questions.a: A medium is the material through which sound propagates, e.g. a desk, water or air. A vacuum is a space with no medium (matter) at all, so sound cannot propagate through it.
s: Medium: material that carries sound, with a correct example
Vacuum: no matter, so no sound propagation

questions.q: A listener on the Moon-like surface of a planet with no atmosphere sees a rock-fall. (a) Will she hear it? (b) Give the reason in terms of what sound needs.
questions.a: (a) She will not hear it. (b) Sound needs a material medium to propagate; with no atmosphere there is nothing to carry the sound to her.
s: (a) She hears nothing
(b) Sound needs a medium and none is present

questions.q: Describe the vacuum bell jar experiment: what is set up, what is done and what is observed, and state the conclusion.
questions.a: An electric bell is placed in a bell jar and switched on, and its loudness is noted. Air is then sucked out of the jar with a vacuum pump; the sound becomes fainter until almost none is heard, though the bell is seen ringing. When air is let back, the sound returns to its former loudness. So sound cannot propagate in a vacuum; it needs a medium.
s: Sets up a ringing bell in a jar connected to a vacuum pump
Observes fading sound as air is removed and return when air is let in
Concludes sound needs a medium

questions.q: Sana says: 'Because the tapping of submerged spoons reached me after travelling through water and air, sound must be able to travel through liquids and gases.' Test her claim.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. The tap was heard after the sound travelled through the water (a liquid) and then the air (a gas), which shows that sound propagates through liquids and gases; the chapter also says it travels through solids.
s: Verdict: Yes
Water carried the sound, so liquids carry sound
Air carried it to her ear, so gases carry sound

questions.q: Kavya says: 'Astronauts on a spacewalk cannot hear clanking metal, so they cannot communicate with each other at all.' Decide whether she is right, wrong or partly right.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that they cannot directly hear speech or clanking, since space is a near vacuum with no medium. She is wrong that they cannot communicate, because they use special devices fitted in their spacesuits.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: no direct hearing in near vacuum
Wrong part: communication happens through suit devices

questions.q: Imran says: 'In the bell jar experiment the sound disappeared, which proves that the bell stopped ringing once air was removed.' Show that this conclusion cannot be drawn from the experiment.
questions.a: In the experiment the bell can still be seen ringing at near vacuum even though almost no sound is heard. So the bell did not stop; the sound fades because there is no medium to carry it, and the conclusion is wrong.
s: Notes the bell is still seen ringing
Explains the sound is not heard because there is no medium
Concludes the bell did not stop, so the claim is false

questions.q: Three activities were done in the chapter: ear on a desk, submerged spoons and the bell jar. For each, state what was done, what was learnt about sound and what the three together allow you to conclude about the word 'medium'.
questions.a: Desk: ear pressed to a desk hears a friend's knock, so sound travels through solids. Spoons: tapped under water and heard, so sound travels through liquids. Bell jar: sound fades as air is pumped out, so sound needs a medium. Together they show a medium can be a solid, a liquid or a gas, but sound cannot travel with none.
s: Desk activity with correct finding (solids)
Spoon activity with correct finding (liquids)
Bell jar finding: needs a medium
Medium can be solid, liquid or gas
Sound cannot propagate without a medium (vacuum)

questions.q: Write a short note of five points for Class 6 students explaining why two astronauts cannot talk directly to each other on a spacewalk. Use the words medium, vacuum and propagate, and say how they do communicate.
questions.a: Sound is produced by vibrations of a source. It must propagate through a medium such as a solid, liquid or gas. Outer space is a near vacuum, so no medium is present. Hence the astronauts cannot directly hear each other or the clank of metal. They communicate through special devices fitted into their spacesuits.
s: Sound is produced by a vibrating source
Needs a medium to propagate
Space is a near vacuum with no medium
So no direct hearing
Special devices in suits for communication

questions.q:
A Class 9 group repeats the bell jar experiment and writes down how the sound seemed at four stages. Stage 1: jar full of air, bell very loud. Stage 2: pump running for a while, bell faint. Stage 3: pump running longer, bell almost inaudible but the bell is seen ringing. Stage 4: air let back in, bell loud again. One student suggests writing the conclusion as 'sound needs air'. Another suggests 'sound needs a medium'. They also did the desk and spoon activities earlier.
(a) Which stage corresponds to a near vacuum?
(b) What do the students see at that stage that tells them the bell has not stopped?
(c) What does Stage 4 show about the sound?
(d) Which conclusion, 'needs air' or 'needs a medium', is better supported by all the activities done, and what does the other one wrongly leave out?
questions.a: (a) Stage 3. (b) The bell can still be seen ringing. (c) The sound returns and gradually becomes as loud as before, so the loss at Stage 3 was due to missing air. (d) 'Needs a medium' is better because the desk (solid) and spoons (liquid) show sound travels in non-gaseous media too; 'needs air' wrongly leaves out solids and liquids.
s: (a) Stage 3 near vacuum
(b) Bell still seen ringing
(c) Sound gradually returns
(d) Chooses medium and notes solids and liquids also carry sound

questions.q:
A film shows a spacecraft exploding in outer space. The audience is meant to hear a loud blast at the very moment the fireball appears. The sound engineer says the blast should be left out entirely because the scene is set in space, while the director says the audience will feel the film is dull without it. The two astronauts shown nearby are talking to each other as if on a street.
(a) Why would the blast not be heard by anyone in space?
(b) What error is there in the astronauts talking 'as if on a street'?
(c) Which device does the chapter say real astronauts use, and where is it fitted?
(d) The director can show the explosion silent, or add the blast and tell viewers it is only for effect. Choose one and say what is gained and what is lost.
questions.a: (a) Outer space is a near vacuum, so there is no medium for sound to propagate. (b) Astronauts cannot directly hear each other speak in space. (c) Special devices fitted into their spacesuits. (d) A reasoned choice: silence is true to the science but may seem dull; adding the blast is dramatic but not correct unless explained.
s: (a) No medium in near vacuum
(b) No direct speech in space
(c) Special devices in spacesuits
(d) Reasoned choice with one gain and one loss

questions.q: Kiran and a friend hold the two ends of a slinky, with a red mark on one turn near the middle. Kiran gives a sharp push and pull and a disturbance travels to the friend's end. What does the red mark do?
questions.a: It oscillates to and fro about its own rest position, parallel to the direction of the disturbance
o: It oscillates to and fro about its own rest position, parallel to the direction of the disturbance
It travels along with the disturbance and finally reaches the far end held by the friend
It moves up and down across the line of the slinky as the disturbance passes
It stays perfectly fixed because the turns of a slinky do not move during a disturbance

questions.q: In a long tube of air, a piston has just finished moving backward, away from the air. Which statement describes the air close to the piston at that instant?
questions.a: The air there has lower than average density, a rarefaction, which moves ahead through the tube
o: The air there has lower than average density, a rarefaction, which moves ahead through the tube
The air there has higher than average density, a compression, which stays near the piston
The air there has the average density, as nothing has changed in the tube
The air particles there have moved all the way to the open end of the tube

questions.q: A student draws four sketches of a wave. In each she draws one arrow for the direction in which the wave moves and another for the direction in which the particles of the medium vibrate. Which sketch represents a sound wave?
questions.a: Both arrows lie along the same straight line
o: Both arrows lie along the same straight line
The two arrows are at right angles to each other
The particle arrow points opposite to the wave arrow with no motion along it
The particle arrow rotates in a circle around the wave arrow

questions.q: A firecracker is burst 30 m from a stretched balloon sheet, and rice grains sprinkled on the sheet jump. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: Sound waves carried energy through the air to the sheet, which then vibrated and moved the grains
o: Sound waves carried energy through the air to the sheet, which then vibrated and moved the grains
Air particles from the firecracker travelled all the way to the sheet and pushed the grains
The light from the firecracker, and not its sound, shook the sheet and the grains
The sheet began vibrating by itself, because sound is not a form of energy at all

questions.q: A singer's voice enters a microphone at a school function. Which change takes place inside the microphone?
questions.a: Sound waves make a thin diaphragm vibrate, and these vibrations become an electrical signal
o: Sound waves make a thin diaphragm vibrate, and these vibrations become an electrical signal
An electrical signal makes a cone vibrate inside it and so produces the sound again
The sound energy is stored unchanged as sound inside the body of the microphone
Light from the stage is turned into the electrical signal that is sent out

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: In a sound wave the particles of the medium vibrate about their mean positions.
Statement 2: A rarefaction is a region where the density is higher than the average density.
Statement 3: A small source in open air sends out spherical waves, spreading in all directions.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false: a rarefaction is a region of lower than average density; higher density is a compression.
o: 1 and 3 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A sound wave in air is a transverse wave.
Reason (R): Sound needs a material medium to propagate.
questions.a: A is false: the particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation, so sound is a longitudinal wave. R is true, because sound is a mechanical wave.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q: A piston in a tube moves backward and the air next to it becomes less dense than the average. The region of lower density is called a ___.
questions.a: rarefaction

questions.q:
As a sound wave passes through air, individual air particles only vibrate about their mean positions, and it is the disturbance that moves forward.
State True or False and give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: True. In the slinky and piston models, each turn or particle oscillates about its own position, while the compression or rarefaction passes from one particle to the next by collisions.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: particles oscillate in place and the disturbance travels

questions.q:
(a) Name the two kinds of region that an oscillating piston creates in the air of a tube.
(b) State which one is formed during the forward motion of the piston and why it forms.
questions.a: (a) Compressions and rarefactions. (b) A compression forms during the forward motion, because the piston pushes nearby air particles together, so the air there has higher than average density.
s: (a) Compression and rarefaction
(b) Compression on forward motion, due to higher density

questions.q: Differentiate between a longitudinal wave and a transverse wave in terms of the particles' direction of vibration, and state which type sound is.
questions.a: In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation; in a transverse wave they vibrate perpendicular to it. Sound is a longitudinal wave.
s: Parallel for longitudinal, perpendicular for transverse
Sound is longitudinal

questions.q:
(a) State the energy change that takes place in a microphone.
(b) Describe the change that a speaker brings about, and how it relates to the microphone's.
questions.a: (a) A microphone converts sound energy into electrical energy. (b) A speaker does the opposite: an electrical signal makes its cone or diaphragm vibrate and produce sound.
s: (a) Sound to electrical
(b) Electrical signal vibrates cone, producing sound; the reverse of the microphone

questions.q: In Activity 10.6 the beater strikes a metal plate near a sheet stretched over a bowl, without touching it, and the rice grains on the sheet jump. Explain why this happens.
questions.a: The vibrating plate transfers energy to the air, the sound propagates through the air to the sheet and makes it vibrate, and the vibrating sheet moves the grains.
s: Sound travels through air from the plate to the sheet
Energy of sound makes the sheet vibrate and move the grains

questions.q: Explain how a slinky pushed and pulled at one end can be used as an analogy for sound travelling in air. Include what the closer turns, the spread-out turns and a marked turn represent.
questions.a: The closer-together turns represent a region of higher density of air (a compression) and the more spread-out turns represent lower density (a rarefaction); these regions travel along the slinky. A marked turn only oscillates about its own position, as air particles do while the sound passes.
s: Closer turns are compression, spread out turns are rarefaction
These regions travel along the slinky
Marked turn oscillates in place like air particles

questions.q: Bhavna says: 'When I speak to my friend across the room, the air particles that leave my mouth travel across the room and carry my words.' Test her claim.
questions.a: No, the claim is wrong. In a sound wave, the particles of the medium only vibrate about their mean positions; they do not travel with the wave. It is the disturbance of compressions and rarefactions, carrying energy, that moves across the room.
s: Verdict: No
Particles only vibrate about mean positions
It is the disturbance and energy that move across

questions.q: Arun says: 'Sound is a mechanical wave because it needs a material medium to propagate, whereas light, which can travel through vacuum, is not a mechanical wave.' Test his claim.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. Waves that require a material medium are mechanical, and sound is one; the chapter says light, a transverse wave, can travel through vacuum, so it is not a mechanical wave.
s: Verdict: Yes
Sound needs a medium so it is mechanical
Light travels through vacuum so it is not mechanical

questions.q: A small bell is rung in the middle of an open field. Explain why the sound reaches listeners all around it, whereas the sound made by the piston in a tube is shown moving in only one direction.
questions.a: A small source in open air sets neighbouring particles vibrating in all directions, so compressions and rarefactions spread as spherical waves. In the tube the air is confined and the piston is only an idealised model, drawn as moving one way for simplicity.
s: Particles collide with neighbours in all directions in open air
Waves spread as spherical waves
Piston-tube model shown in one direction for simplicity

questions.q: Using the model of an oscillating piston in a tube, explain how a sound wave is set up. Your answer must say how a compression forms, how a rarefaction forms, how they travel along the tube and what the air particles themselves do.
questions.a: When the piston moves forward it pushes nearby particles together, forming a compression of higher than average density. When it moves back, the air near it becomes less dense, forming a rarefaction. The compressed particles collide with neighbours and pass the compression forward; the rarefaction likewise moves ahead. Particles only vibrate about their mean positions, so the alternating compressions and rarefactions travel without any flow of air.
s: Forward motion forms a compression
Backward motion forms a rarefaction
Collisions pass the disturbance forward
Particles vibrate about mean positions, no flow of air
Alternating compressions and rarefactions together are the sound wave

questions.q: A student writes: 'Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave that carries energy.' Justify each of the four terms 'longitudinal', 'mechanical', 'wave' and 'carries energy' with one piece of evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Longitudinal: particles vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation. Mechanical: it needs a material medium and cannot propagate in vacuum. Wave: a disturbance of alternating compressions and rarefactions propagates without flow of particles. Carries energy: in Activity 10.6 the sound makes a sheet vibrate and the grains jump. Energy, not particles, is transferred.
s: Longitudinal justified by parallel vibration
Mechanical justified by need of a medium
Wave justified by travelling compressions and rarefactions
Energy justified by the grain activity
States that energy, not particles, is transferred

questions.q:
A teacher fits a thin balloon sheet tightly over a wide bowl and sprinkles rice grains evenly on it. (c) What would she observe if the bowl and plate were inside a jar from which air has been removed? Give the reason.
(d) Choose between the plate and the speaker for repeating the activity ten times in the same way, and give one advantage and one limit of your choice.
questions.a: (a) The sound travels through the air to the sheet and makes it vibrate, which moves the grains. (b) Energy; in sound propagation the energy is transferred, not the particles of the medium. (c) The grains would not move, since sound cannot propagate without a medium. (d) A reasoned choice: the speaker gives a repeatable volume but needs a power source and converts electrical energy; the plate is simple and loud but each strike may differ.
s: (a) Sound travels through air and vibrates the sheet
(b) Energy is transferred, not particles
(c) Grains do not move in near vacuum because there is no medium
(d) Reasoned choice with one advantage and one limit

questions.q:
A teacher can teach how sound travels using either a slinky or the model of a piston oscillating in a tube of air. In the piston model, the air particles are drawn as dots, which are too small and quick to see in real life. A tube and piston are more costly than a slinky.
(a) In the slinky model, what represents the compressions, and what does the marked turn show?

questions.a: (a) The closer-together turns represent a region of higher density, a compression; the marked turn oscillates about its own position, parallel to the disturbance. (b) A rarefaction. (c) The medium does not travel with the wave; particles only vibrate about their mean positions. (d) A reasoned choice: the slinky is cheap and visible but is only an analogy; the piston model is closer to air and shows density changes but is harder to see.
s: (a) Closer turns are compressions; marked turn oscillates in place
(b) Rarefaction
(c) The medium does not travel with the wave
(d) Reasoned choice with what the other model explains better

questions.q:

questions.q: In the density against distance graph of a sound wave, which feature corresponds to a compression and which to a rarefaction? State what the density is, compared with the average, at each.
questions.a: The crest, the highest point, corresponds to a compression and has the maximum density, above the average; the trough, the lowest point, corresponds to a rarefaction and has the minimum density, below the average.

questions.q:

questions.q: Describe how the variation of density in a sound wave is shown on a graph. Name what is plotted on each axis, what the horizontal dashed line shows, and what the crest and trough are.
questions.a: Distance from the source is plotted on the x-axis and the density of the medium on the y-axis. The dashed horizontal line marks the average density. The highest point, the crest, is the maximum density (in a compression); the lowest point, the trough, is the minimum density (in a rarefaction).
s: Axes: distance on x, density on y
Dashed line is the average density
Crest is maximum and trough is minimum density

questions.q: Rahul says: 'A sound of time period 0.5 s has a frequency of 0.5 Hz.' Test his claim.
questions.a: No, the claim is wrong. Frequency = 1/time period = 1/0.5 = 2 Hz. He has copied the period in place of taking its inverse.
s: Verdict: No
Uses frequency = 1/T
Correct value 2 Hz

questions.q: On a graph with consecutive crests at 1.5 cm and 4.5 cm, Mini says: 'The wavelength is 3.0 cm, and the distance from a crest to the very next trough is also 3.0 cm.' Decide whether she is right, wrong or partly right.

questions.a: Yes, she is right. Frequency = 1/0.01 = 100 Hz, which means 100 oscillations each second, so in 60 s there are 100 x 60 = 6000 oscillations.
s: Verdict: Yes
Frequency is 100 Hz
6000 oscillations in 60 s

questions.q: A student says that she measured a sound with frequency 4 Hz and time period 4 s. Show that these two values cannot belong to the same sound.

s: States the inverse relation between frequency and period
Computes 0.25 s for 4 Hz
Concludes the pair is impossible

Intensity falls with distance

(d) A reasoned choice: the 30 m fence fails (difference 0.082 s); the 50 m fence works with a small margin; the 200 m fence gives a bigger margin of 0.55 s but the listener is far away and the teacher must supervise a larger area.
s: (b) 0.137 s, separate
(c) About 36.5 m
(d) Reasoned choice, rejecting 30 m

If a reflected sound reaches a listener only 0.08 s after the original sound, she cannot hear it as a separate sound.

questions.q:
(a) How far does sound travel in 0.1 s at 340 m/s?
(b) Use this to explain why the smallest distance from a reflecting wall for hearing an echo is 17 m and not 34 m.
questions.a: (a) 340 x 0.1 = 34 m. (b) The sound travels from the listener to the wall and back, so 34 m is the total path; the wall is half of this, 17 m, away.
s: (a) 34 m in 0.1 s
(b) Path is to the wall and back, so distance is half, 17 m

questions.q:
A tanpura string has a fundamental frequency of 220 Hz.
(a) What is the frequency of the note one octave above it?
(b) What is the time period of that higher note?
questions.a: (a) An octave is a doubling of frequency, so 2 x 220 = 440 Hz. (b) Time period = 1/440 = about 0.0023 s.
s: (b) About 0.0023 s

questions.q: Differentiate between a tone and a musical note. Give one source of each.
questions.a: A tone is a sound of a single frequency, such as from a tuning fork or oral whistling. A musical note is a combination of a lowest frequency, the fundamental, and higher frequencies, the overtones, as from a plucked tanpura string or a singing voice.
s: Tone: single frequency, with a source
Musical note: fundamental plus overtones, with a source

questions.q: Differentiate between intensity and loudness, saying which of the two depends on the listener.
questions.a: Intensity is a measurable quantity, the sound energy passing per unit area per unit time. Loudness is how a human perceives the amplitude of a sound, commonly measured in decibels, and depends on the listener's hearing ability.
s: Intensity is objective and measurable
Loudness is perception and depends on the listener

questions.q: Name one use of infrasonic waves and one use of ultrasonic waves from the chapter, and say why neither can be used by humans simply by listening.
questions.a: Infrasonic waves are used to detect natural events such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions or storms; ultrasonic waves are used for imaging internal organs (ultrasonography), cleaning, welding or finding flaws in metal. Both lie outside the audible range of 20 Hz to 20 kHz, so humans cannot hear them.
s: One correct use of each
Both lie outside the audible range 20 Hz to 20 kHz

questions.q: Describe how sonar works to find a submarine under water. Say what is sent, what happens to it, and what the operator finds out.
questions.a: Sonar sends ultrasonic waves into the water. They are reflected from the submarine and come back to the ship, and the reflected waves are analysed. This gives the distance (half of speed x total time), the direction and the speed of the object.
s: Ultrasonic waves are sent into water
Reflected waves from the object are received and analysed
Finds distance, direction and speed of the object

questions.q: Rohit says: 'In a small room there is no echo because the walls absorb all the sound that hits them.' Test his reasoning.
questions.a: No, his reason is wrong. Walls reflect sound, but in a small room the reflections come back too quickly, in less than 0.1 s, for the brain to separate them from the original sound, so no echo is heard. Absorption is the property of soft surfaces such as curtains, not of all walls.
s: Verdict: No
Real reason: the gap is less than 0.1 s
Absorbing surfaces are the soft ones, not walls in general

questions.q: Ravi says: 'A siren is of high pitch and thunder is of low pitch, so pitch tells us exactly how many hertz a sound has.' Decide whether he is right, wrong or partly right.
questions.a: Partly right. In general, high pitch sounds such as a siren have higher frequencies and low pitch sounds such as thunder have lower frequencies, so his examples are fine. But the chapter says the exact mathematical relation between pitch and frequency is complicated, so pitch alone does not give the number of hertz.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: high pitch tends to mean higher frequency
Wrong part: the exact relation is complicated, so pitch is not an exact frequency

questions.q: A student says she heard a clear echo of her shout from a wall 10 m away. Take the speed of sound as 340 m/s. Show that this cannot be correct.
questions.a: The sound travels 10 m to the wall and 10 m back, a total of 20 m, which takes 20/340 = about 0.059 s. This is less than 0.1 s, so the brain cannot separate the reflected sound from the original and no clear echo is heard. The wall must be at least 17 m away.

Time about 0.059 s, less than 0.1 s
Concludes that no clear echo is possible below 17 m

questions.q: Write a short report titled 'Sound that we cannot hear'. Give two uses of infrasonic waves, three uses of ultrasonic waves and the range of frequencies that humans can hear, saying what each use does. Close with one example each of an animal that detects infrasound and one that detects ultrasound.
questions.a: Humans hear 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Infrasonic waves (below 20 Hz) detect earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, and severe storms, since they travel long distances through air and the Earth. Ultrasonic waves (above 20 kHz) image internal organs without surgery, break kidney stones, clean machine parts or weld, and find defects in metal blocks. Elephants detect infrasound; bats, dogs, cats or dolphins detect ultrasound.

Two correct uses of infrasonic waves
Three correct uses of ultrasonic waves

questions.q:
A new auditorium in Pune has a stage and a bare, smooth rear wall 34 m behind the speaker. Engineers find that a clap on stage reaches the speaker again from the rear wall after a delay, while reflections from the nearby side panels arrive 0.03 s after the clap. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. The management can cover the rear wall with sound-absorbing panels, or leave it smooth to keep the hall lively.
(a) Find the delay of the reflection from the rear wall.
(b) Say which reflection is an echo and which adds to reverberation, and why.
(c) Name three things the chapter says designers use to reduce reverberation.
(d) Choose to cover the rear wall or leave it bare, and give one advantage and one limit of your choice.
questions.a: (a) Path 34 + 34 = 68 m, so 68/340 = 0.2 s. (b) The rear wall reflection comes after 0.2 s, more than 0.1 s, so it is heard as an echo; the side panel reflections come within 0.05 s, so they add to reverberation. (c) Sound-absorbing panels, upholstered chairs and curtains (soft, porous surfaces). (d) A reasoned choice: covering the wall removes the late echo and keeps speech clear, but too much absorption can make the hall dull and costs more; leaving it bare keeps liveliness but gives a distracting echo.
s: (b) Rear wall echo, side panels reverberation, with reasons
(c) Absorbing panels, upholstered chairs, curtains
(d) Reasoned choice with one advantage and one limit

questions.q:
A fishing boat has a sonar that sends ultrasonic pulses into seawater, where sound travels at 1530 m/s. One pulse is reflected from a shoal of fish and returns after 0.24 s, and another returns from the sea floor after 0.80 s. A minute later, a new pulse from the shoal returns after 0.30 s. The boat's net hangs on a cable that is either 200 m or 250 m long.
(a) How deep is the shoal at the first reading?
(b) How far above the sea floor was the shoal at that time?
(c) How deep is the shoal at the new reading, and what does it show about how the shoal moved?
(d) Choose which cable length to use at the new reading, and say what the other choice would have cost.
questions.a: (a) 1530 x 0.24 / 2 = 183.6 m. (b) The floor is 1530 x 0.80 / 2 = 612 m deep, so the shoal was 612 - 183.6 = 428.4 m above it. (c) 1530 x 0.30 / 2 = 229.5 m; the shoal moved deeper by 45.9 m. (d) The 250 m cable reaches 229.5 m while a 200 m cable falls 29.5 m short and misses the shoal; but the longer cable is heavier and harder to handle.
s: (b) 428.4 m above the floor
(c) 229.5 m, the shoal moved deeper
(d) Reasoned cable choice with the cost of the other
